description: A frightening scene of air pollution and extremely poor visibility in Delhi, India, in December 2019. During the winter months, Delhi, a metropolis with a population of nearly 34.6 million [ 1 ] , becomes engulfed in toxic smog. The main causes of this condition include the burning of crop residue (stubble) in the neighboring states of Punjab and Haryana. These are agrarian states located just north and west of Delhi, where farmers often burn leftover straw after the rice harvest to clear their fields quickly. The smoke drifts into Delhi, where cold winter air tends to stagnate and trap pollutants close to the ground. Urban emissions also play a major role. Dust particles and gases released from vehicles, industries, and construction activities further intensify the pollution. According to scientific studies, breathing Delhi’s air during those days was considered equivalent to smoking about 49 cigarettes [ 2 ] , underscoring the extreme health risks.
